Monomial and Clifford constructions

The first part of this research companion records the direct odd-prime and weighted dyadic construc-
tions, including the low-rank carrier repairs. This continuation returns to the earlier monomial and
Clifford branches. Their conclusions are not interchangeable. A genuine arithmetic candidate may have
the right dimension and conductor while failing to contain a prescribed full simple character. A finite
carrier may have enough dimension while failing the required action or marking. A compatible formal
interface may still await its actual arithmetic input.

The purpose here is to make those distinctions mathematically usable. We extract the precise restricted
implications, explain the negative results, and retain the surviving routes. The presentation includes
elementary proofs where the argument is short enough to expose completely. Deeper arithmetic state-
ments are identified as inherited ordinary arguments with named classical inputs. No theorem in this
continuation is newly certified by Lean.

Source provenance. The first part of this companion is retained from a preserved reader. Its complete
editable source archive was not recovered. The monomial and Clifford analysis uses the retained
initial research archive. The source map records this boundary. This book does not claim to
reconstruct unavailable source files.


Mathematical scope. Conjecture 66 remains the general arithmetic realization obligation, with the
same-candidate H5 comparison kept separate. The positive constructions below are restricted statements.
The negative examples refute specified shortcuts or prescribed candidates, not the entire conjecture.

Conductors and native markings

A conductor is an arithmetic invariant, not a complete description of a type. A nondegenerate commuta-
tor is a finite invariant, not a complete description of a marked dyadic extension. These two distinctions
meet at the smallest dyadic construction with exactly enough quotient capacity. There is no spare plane
there to absorb an independently prescribed quadratic mismatch.

This continuation audits the conductor and marking branches at their actual hypotheses. It keeps three
arithmetic objects separate: the original source representation, a candidate obtained through a classical
induction and descent construction, and a candidate arising from a proposed explicit type. A compari-
son is useful only when its normalization and its subject are fixed.

The resulting finite theory is also constructive. A discrepancy between two quadratic refinements be-
comes one linear functional. When its Arf obstruction vanishes, a single transvection gives an explicit
correction. For a supplied odd-order finite action, a further central discrepancy can be removed by a
finite sum. Neither correction constructs the missing arithmetic action, chooses a canonical native mark-
ing, or settles the full phase equations.

Source provenance. The conductor and marking analysis retains the earlier parts’ source and review
boundaries. In particular, the first part is available as a preserved reader, while its complete editable
archive remains unavailable. The evidence ledger distinguishes this documentary gap from the
unresolved mathematical obligations.

Evidence status. Ordinary finite proofs are supplied below. The arithmetic construction records are
inherited arguments audited against selected primary statements. Recorded exact tests check finite
models and normalizations. No fresh Lean compilation or external peer review is claimed.
